slides.heading: Put your priority first
slides.body: Same-day lifting and intervals can work when you recover well.
slides.narration: You can do HIIT and weights on the same day if you recover well. This short video accompanies the IZEM guide. If you're already used to both, put your main training goal first. Lift first when strength is the priority. Do your key interval session first when conditioning matters more. This is a planning starting point, not a rule that produces better results for everyone.

slides.heading: Start gradually
slides.body: Two demanding workouts are not a starting requirement.
slides.narration: If you're new to exercise, build up gradually rather than stacking two hard sessions. With a chronic condition, ask about appropriate activity. If you've been inactive, check with a clinician before starting vigorous exercise. The article links to current CDC guidance. General fitness advice cannot establish your medical readiness.

slides.heading: One visit or two windows
slides.body: Allow time for your planned work, rest and recovery.
slides.narration: One gym visit and two separate sessions are different choices. With one visit, allow time for your warm-up, lifting rests and a gradual finish. If the interval workout only fits by rushing that work, move it. A morning and evening arrangement gives you time to rest, eat and drink, but it does not make excessive total training manageable.

slides.heading: No universal hour gap
slides.body: Research comparisons are not a personal recovery guarantee.
slides.narration: There is no single recovery interval established as enough for every person. A nine-week study in twenty-nine moderately active men separated the concurrent sessions by about three hours. Both orders supported strength and lean mass gains, while some power outcomes differed. The study does not establish an ideal schedule for everyone. Experienced lifters and athletes training power need particular care with demanding combinations.

slides.heading: Count the actual workload
slides.body: Easy cardio, intervals and loaded circuits differ.
slides.narration: In this guide, HIIT means hard aerobic intervals separated by recovery, such as repeated efforts on a stationary bike. Easy cardio has a different demand. A loaded circuit also adds resistance work. Count it when reviewing your lifting workload. Use an activity you already know and can perform well. Do not add unfamiliar explosive movements just because a workout calls them a finisher.

slides.heading: Review your next workout
slides.body: Record completed work and choose one adjustment.
slides.narration: Record your main goal, lifting loads and reps, interval work and recovery periods. Then compare planned and completed work at your next comparable workout. If the same work repeatedly gets harder or you keep missing the intended effort, reduce or move the second session before adding more. Also consider sleep, food, stress and your other training. One difficult day does not identify the cause. Do not push through pain; pain and persistent symptoms need appropriate assessment.

slides.heading: Read the complete guide
slides.body: Use the planning table, worked examples and copyable log.
slides.narration: The complete article includes a scheduling table, hypothetical examples, a copyable training log and linked research with its limits. IZEM offers plans based on your schedule and equipment, set and rep logging, and supported workout changes. Describe the additional interval work when asking for coaching guidance. The app provides general fitness guidance and does not replace a clinician or an in-person technique assessment. Read the guide at youraicoach dot life.
